newsitem.title: TAIWAN: In hint of thaw, Taiwan announces China visit.
newsitem.headline: In hint of thaw, Taiwan announces China visit.

text.p: Taiwan said on Wednesday a senior negotiator whose organisation handles talks with Beijing would visit rival China in late April, signalling a modest easing of a 22-month-old impasse.

"We have obtained verbal agreement from the mainland side, agreeing to visits by the deputy secretaries general," said Lee Ching-ping, deputy secretary-general of Taipei's semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation.
Lee said he and his delegation would start a 10-day visit to Beijing, Zhengzhou, Chengdu and Shanghai on April 28.
Senior officials welcomed Beijing's decision to allow the exchange, the state-run Central News Agency reported.
A furious China froze talks between the Taipei foundation and its Beijing counterpart after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui made a landmark private visit to the United States in mid-1995.

Communist China, which has viewed Nationalist Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, said Lee Teng-hui's U.S. visit showed that he sought independence for the island rather than reunification with the mainland.
Despite a stream of private exchanges across the Taiwan Strait, some involving senior mainland bureaucrats, China had rejected visits by leaders of the Straits Exchange Foundation.

Lee Ching-ping, who led a delegation to China in June 1995 before such contacts collapsed, said he was inviting his counterpart, Liu Gangqi of the Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits, to visit Taiwan.
"We had reached a consensus that Liu should also lead a cultural and educational delegation to Taiwan," Lee said.
"If I can go this time, I will formally invite him to visit Taiwan on behalf of the Straits Exchange Foundation."
Lee's delegation will meet Chinese officials to discuss potential problems arising from an earlier agreement on authentication of cross-strait documents.
As before, the contacts will be considered unofficial by both sides, as neither side recognises the other's sovereignty.
Relations across the strait remain frosty.

Beijing rattled Taiwan with war games and missile tests in waters near the island in the run-up to the island's March 1996 presidential election -- the first time a Chinese government has chosen its leader through popular suffrage.
Beijing acknowledged the eight months of manoeuvres were a bid to intimidate Taiwan voters against seeking independence.
Taiwan has repeatedly urged China to resume talks to resolve thorny issues facing both sides, including fishing disputes, repatriation of hijackers and stowaways.

Beijing has declined, saying no talks were possible until Taiwan showed its sincerity by halting its drive to enter the United Nations, its courtship of ties with other countries and other "splittist" activities.
